findings.F1: The tested surge idea is too small to show here: across all 6 coins and grid cells with a positive 30-day return, the 10-day excess return rises from -1.5 % (t -1.43, 117 cases) in the lowest surge quintile to +2.2 % to +3.3 % (t 1.12 to 1.75, 126 to 139 cases) in the top three quintiles, and no quintile reaches t 2; with a negative 30-day return every surge quintile is slightly negative (-0.5 % to -1.1 %, |t| < 0.85).
findings.F2: Nearness to the 30-day high carries a 10-day move the surge does not explain: on the grid starting at each window's first row, cells in each coin's top quintile of close over its 30-day highest close are followed by a 10-day excess return of +3.9 % (t 3.02, 278 cases), against -0.1 % to -3.0 % in the four lower quintiles; on the 5-day horizon the same top quintile gives +2.3 % (t 2.67).
findings.F3: The nearness effect is not robust to where the grid starts: on the grid shifted by 5 days, the same top quintile gives +1.5 % (t 1.35, 287 cases). The within-coin Spearman correlation of nearness with the 10-day excess is weak (-0.04 to +0.12, no p below 0.06), and earlier runs already found nearness to highs pays (findings F3, F9). F2 is therefore at best a modest, graded effect at the top end only.
findings.F4: Nearness and a strong 7-day return reinforce each other. Cells in both top quintiles are followed by +7.4 % excess over 10 days (t 2.97, 130 cases), against +0.8 % (t 0.83, 148) for near-high alone, +0.6 % (t 0.44, 148) for a top 7-day return alone, and -1.5 % (t -3.32, 960) for neither.
findings.F5: The 7-day return alone sorts the next 10 days on the first grid: -2.1 % to -1.6 % excess in the lowest three quintiles (t about -2.1 to -2.4), +3.7 % (t 2.76, 278) in the top quintile. On the shifted grid the top quintile falls to +1.1 % (t 1.03), so it is weaker than F4.
findings.F6: Nearness scaled by the coin's 30-day volatility sorts like raw nearness. Its top quintile gives +4.0 % (t 3.05) on the first grid and +1.9 % (t 1.63) on the shifted grid, the most stable of the nearness measures across the two grids.
findings.F7: The near-high effect is concentrated in the earlier years and in some coins. The top quintile gives +6.8 % (t 3.22, 116 cases) before 2022 and +1.8 % (t 1.12, 162) from 2022. By coin it gives +11.8 % for XRP (t 2.62), +2.2 % to +2.4 % for BTC and ETH (t 1.27 to 1.58), and +0.6 % to +0.7 % for LTC and XMR.
findings.F8: The book's year and window results follow the coins. Its mean daily return is negative in 2018 (-0.19 %) and 2022 (-0.08 %), as are the coins' (-0.35 %, -0.18 %). Its largest windows (+131 %, +113 %) are those where the coins rose most (+281 %, +87 %), so its Calmar failure comes from shared down years, not from surges.
findings.F9: The moves in F2 and F4 are large against a trade: a 10-day excess of +3.9 % to +7.4 % per case is 20 to 39 times the 0.19 % round-trip cost of this backtest. Size is not the obstacle; robustness across grid offsets (F3) and years (F7) is.

ideas.idea: The closer a coin's hourly close is to its highest close of the last 30 days, the more it rises over the next 10 days above its usual 10-day return, and the more so the larger its 7-day return.
ideas.consequence: A trader would hold a coin for about ten days when it trades at its monthly high after a strong week, and refuse long entries in coins far below their monthly high after a weak week.
ideas.name: strong week at monthly high

ideas.idea: The closer a coin's hourly close is to its highest close of the last 30 days, measured in units of its 30-day hourly volatility, the more it rises over the next 10 days above its usual 10-day return.
ideas.consequence: A trader would favour ten-day longs in coins sitting within a small number of their own usual moves of the monthly high, and give less weight to coins further below it.
ideas.name: volatility-scaled nearness to high
